name: Roraima
summary_text: Roraima stands under Brazil's national framework rather than its own state statute. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 removed surgery, hormones or a diagnosis as conditions for changing a name and gender marker. No state-level deviation from those provisions is recorded for Roraima, and a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 and MI 4733 that discrimination and violence motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity constitute a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment of one to five years and fines. An OAB/SP guide for expatriates places these among the most progressive LGBTQ protections in Latin America on paper, while stating plainly that enforcement is uneven in practice.  Identity documents follow the national rules. There is no third-gender option on documents nationwide, though civil-registry entries recording a non-binary or unspecified gender have been possible since 2020 and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of a registry entry to a neutral gender as precedent. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.  Arrest carries a specific placement regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and the judge must consult the person on whether they prefer a female, male or LGBTI-specific unit and, within it, the general population or a specific wing or cell. LGBTI-specific spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  The protective text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International reports that Brazil retains one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities in the world, particularly affecting trans people, and that its legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Outright's country overview records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.  Where in the country a visitor is matters to daily exposure. Major cities including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are described as broadly welcoming, with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. Boa Vista and Roraima's other centres are not among the cities identified as having that infrastructure.

name: Santa Catarina
summary_text: Santa Catarina stands under the national framework of Brazil. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, and joint and second-parent adoption were confirmed by the Supreme Federal Tribunal in RE 846.102 (2015). A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.  Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punishable as equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989 following the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2019 ruling in ADO 26. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically in visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes.  Santa Catarina's own constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Trans-specific protection in the state rests on the national constitutional and criminal provisions rather than on the wording of the state charter.  Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. The Superior Court of Justice has ruled that non-binary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity, and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.  Courts in the state have applied family protection to foreign partners. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian.  A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide.  The wider national environment remains contested. A deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013, while constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions continue to apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina.  On health care, the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee in September 2025, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.
